query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a pack cementation aluminization treatment to refractory high-entropy alloys will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, dense Al2O3 scale that enhances high-temperature oxygen resistance by reducing oxygen ingress.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy in its as-cast or as-sintered state that forms mixed oxide scales (e.g., Cr-based oxides and CrTaO4) under high-temperature oxidation, without a protective alumina layer.
generation.intervention: Perform a pack cementation aluminization treatment to introduce additional aluminum into the surface layer of the alloy.
generation.conditions: Exposure at approximately 1100°C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere (e.g., air) for durations around 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, dense Al2O3 scale formed on the alloy’s surface.
generation.mechanism: The treatment increases the local Al concentration at the surface, accelerating the formation of a thermodynamically stable and low-diffusivity Al2O3 layer. This oxide acts as a barrier that slows both the inward diffusion of oxygen and the outward diffusion of metal cations, thereby mitigating further oxidation of the base alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated samples, the treated alloy will show a lower oxidation rate, evidenced by reduced weight gain and a thinner, more adherent oxide scale primarily composed of Al2O3.
generation.baseline: Untreated alloys under similar high-temperature conditions tend to form mixed oxide scales (inclusive of Cr-based oxides and CrTaO4) that are less effective at hindering oxygen diffusion.
generation.boundary: This improvement is anticipated for exposure conditions up to around 1300°C in oxygen-rich environments; outside this range, the behavior and efficacy of the protective alumina scale remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of the protective scale formation, its long-term stability beyond 100 hours, and any potential adverse effects on the alloy’s mechanical properties warrant further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory high-entropy alloy samples: one set treated via pack cementation aluminization and one untreated control. Expose both sets in air at 1100°C for 100 hours. Post-exposure, measure weight gain over time, analyze oxide scale thickness and continuity via cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and use X-ray diffraction (XRD) to identify the oxide phases.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and microstructural integrity
Phase composition of the oxide scale (confirmation of continuous Al2O3 formation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation rate (weight gain), a thinner and more adherent oxide scale, and predominantly Al2O3 formation compared with the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Data for parabolic rate constants of various oxides demonstrates the superiority of Al2O3 and SiO2 scales over other oxides []. Al2O3 and SiO2 are highly stable and exhibit low diffusivities for cations and anions. Al2O3 has small deviations from stoichiometry, low point defect concentrations, and high melting point (2050 °C). SiO2 is more permeable to oxygen and nitrogen than alumina at high temperature and has a lower melting temperature []. The activation energy for diffusion of oxygen in silica is lower than in alumina. Thus, alumina becomes less effective oxidation barrier than silica as temperature is increased. Nevertheless, Al2O3 is an excellent barrier to penetration by oxygen and grows at a slower rate than silica at temperatures to about 1300 °C. Alumina and/or SiO2 scales would be desirable to form on Nb-silicide based alloys. The activity of Al required for the formation of Al2O3 cannot be provided by the Al concentration in the Nb-silicide based alloys owing to the effect of the latter on mechanical behaviour at low and high temperatures. Formation of SiO2 is more likely but depends on alloy microstructure and the formation of Nb2O5 on the scale (see below).

cited_evidence.text: The surface oxidation morphology of CoCrNiAlX (X = 0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7) is shown in Figure 12. It can be seen that there is a clear difference among the alloys. As shown in Figure 12a,b, the oxide layer of the Al0 and Al0.1 alloys has a loose hollow structure, resulting in large-scale spalling on the oxidized surface, as shown by the yellow arrows in the picture. The insets in Figure 12a,b are the magnified morphology of regions A and C. Regions A and C are regions where spinel phases exist. Combining the chemical compositions of different regions of the oxidized surface in Table 6 and the XRD analysis of the surface oxidation products in Figure 10, spinel phases dominated by (Co, Ni) Cr2O4 and NiCrO3 were formed. The B area contains more Cr and O elements, mainly Cr2O3. As the Al content increases, Al2O3 particles begin to appear in the D area, and then a dense Al2O3 film begins to form, preventing further oxidation of the matrix by oxygen, and the spalling situation is alleviated. A large number of Al2O3 particles is formed on the surface of the Al0.3 alloy, as shown in Figure 12c, indicating that Al diffuses rapidly from the matrix to the surface of the oxide layer.
